newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary sees further credit rating upgradings.
newsitem.headline: Hungary sees further credit rating upgradings.

text.p: Continued improvements in the economy should lead to even better credit ratings following a decision by Standard & Poor's to give Hungary a long-awaited investment grade on Monday, the country's top bankers said.
S&P raised its rating on the National Bank of Hungary's long-term foreign currency denominated debt to triple-B minus -- the lowest investment grade -- from double-B plus.
"The upgrading is a very serious and clearly positive signal...," National Bank of Hungary President Gyorgy Suranyi told reporters on Tuesday.
Vice-President Frigyes Harshegyi added that economic figures would even justify a better credit rating.
"I am convinced that further improvement could come next year if we will meet budget targets," he said.
Moody's Investors Service also said recently that it may upgrade NBH debt to investment grade in the next few months, Suranyi said.

Hungary has radically reduced its budget and current account deficits as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP) and state expenditures are likely to drop below 50 percent of GDP in the near future, Suranyi added.

Inflation is still high, but was cut to 22.2 percent year-on-year by September from 31 percent at the middle of last year. Net foreign debt fell below $14 billion from over $20 billion in the middle of last year.
Foreign capital inflow exceeds the current account deficit and international reserves are high, which enables Hungary to cut its foreign debt further.

Suranyie added that the country was not likely to need financing from abroad until the end of next year and it decided to repay credits of some $1 billion before maturity in the near future. Credits to be repaid include loans from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
